notes.meaning: Xerxes gives the entire estate of Haman to Esther as payback for the danger Haman caused her. Esther also reveals that Mordecai is her cousin and the guardian who raised her, which earns Mordecai direct access to the royal court.

The king gives Mordecai the royal signet ring that used to belong to Haman, effectively placing him in the highest office in the empire. Esther then puts Mordecai in charge of managing Haman's vast estate on her behalf.

Even though Esther and Mordecai are now safe and wealthy, the death warrant against all other Jews still stands. Esther risks entering the king's presence again and weeps at his feet, pleading for him to stop Haman's deadly plan.
Xerxes holds out his golden scepter to show Esther that he welcomes her approach and pardons her uninvited visit. Esther then stands up from the floor to present her petition.

Esther speaks with great respect and care, asking the king to cancel the written orders to wipe out the Jews. She wisely places all the guilt on Haman rather than blaming the king who allowed the decree.
Esther explains that her personal safety means nothing if her entire family and nation are slaughtered. Her grief shows deep love and loyalty to her people in their hour of need.

The king reminds Esther and Mordecai of how much goodwill he has already shown by giving them Haman's property and executing Haman. He points to these acts to reassure them that he wants to help protect the Jews.

Xerxes tells Esther and Mordecai to write a new decree and seal it with his signet ring. Under Persian law, an official decree sealed with the king's ring could never be canceled, so they must draft a second law to counter the first one.

The royal scribes assemble about two months after Haman's decree to write down Mordecai's new orders. The messages are translated into the unique language and writing style of every group across all 127 provinces, including the Jews themselves.

Mordecai writes the decree in the king's name and presses the royal seal into the wax to make it official law. He sends riders on the fastest horses from the royal stables so the news will spread across the empire without delay.

The new law grants the Jews in every town the right to gather, bear arms, and defend their lives. They are allowed to strike down anyone who attacks them and take their belongings, reversing the violent threat Haman had arranged.

The decree sets the defense for the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar. This matches the exact day Haman had chosen by casting lots, giving the Jews months to organize and prepare.

Copies of the order are posted in public squares throughout every province so all citizens can read them. This public notice warns potential attackers to back off and lets the Jews know they have the full legal right to protect themselves.
Messengers dash out on royal steeds with great urgency under direct orders from the palace. At the same time, the decree is officially published inside the capital city of Susa.

Mordecai steps out from the palace dressed in royal robes of blue and white, wearing a purple cloak and a gold crown. Unlike the confusion caused by Haman's decree, the city of Susa erupts with loud cheering and joy.
The Jewish people experience light and joy, trading months of fear and grief for gladness and public honor. God turns their season of impending doom into a celebration of hope.

Every province and city celebrates with banquets and holidays as soon as the royal decree arrives. Seeing how God turned the tables to protect His people, many local residents convert to the Jewish faith out of deep respect.
